blocks.text: V. The fifth passage is Iob. XXXVIII, 32., where the Chaldee in the Venetian and Basel editions has וזגתא על אפרחהא תדברנון, And will you lead the hen with her chicks? Literally, over her chicks. But over the chicks means with the chicks. So Deuter. XXII, 6. You shall not take the mother over the young, i.e. with the young. The hen is זגתא, as in the Talmudic tractate Bechoroth ch. 1, fol. 8. 2: אייתו לה תרי ביעי אמר ליה הי דוגתא אוכמתי והי דוגתא חיוורתי, When two eggs were brought, he said to him: That egg is of a black hen, and this one of a white hen. Nor is זגתא pronounced Zagtha, as [II, 680] some think, but Zaggatha. For it belongs to the verbs that double the second radical, like the Arabic name of the hen, دجاجة [dajāja] degiagia, which they derive from the verb دج [dajja] daggia, that is, to walk gently. I think it is formed from the bird's call, which different people render differently. Or from the Chaldee זגג, with Zain and Daleth interchanged, which is customary in those languages. For the rest, beware of understanding an ordinary hen in the paraphrase of Job. For it is a matter of the celestial one, which in the vernacular is called pullicenaria [hen with chicks], by the Greeks Πλειὰς [Pleias] or Πλειάδες [Pleiades], and by the Latins Vergiliae ^{(2)}. But the Hebrew has ועיש על בניה תנחם, and will you lead עיש with its sons? And in that passage עיש is plainly something other than the Pleiades. Namely, עיש is the same as עש in Iob. IX, 9. And עש as is formed by ἀφαίρεσιν [aphairesin] from the Arabic نعش [naʿsh] nas, as an initial N often drops out. Thus גיא gia, splendour, from נגה naga, to shine; גר gar, river, from נגר nagar, to flow; שיא si, or שאת seeth, elevation, from נשה nasa, to lift up; שיג sig, pursuit, from נשג nasag, to pursue or overtake. Further, for the Arabs نعش [naʿsh] nas is first a bier: as in Luc. VII, 14. and in Eutychius of Alexandria p. 277; then the constellation of the bear. Thus for the astrologers النعش الكبري [al-naʿsh al-kubrī] is the greater bier, that is, the Great Bear; النعش الصغري [al-naʿsh al-ṣughrī] the lesser bier, that is, the Little Bear. Namely, four stars arranged [col. 114] in a square are regarded by them as a bier, or coffin, on which a corpse is carried out. And the three following (for us the bear's tail) are for them the daughters, or sons, who accompany the funeral. Alcamus: بنات نعش الكبري سبعة كواكب اربعة منها نعش وثلاث بنات [banāt naʿsh al-kubrī sabʿat kawākib arbaʿa minhā naʿsh wa-thalāth banāt] The daughters of the greater bier: of which four are the bier, and three are the daughters. And elsewhere: الحية كواكب ما بين الغرقدين وبنات نعش [al-ḥayya kawākib mā bayn al-gharqadayn wa-banāt naʿsh] The Serpent (or Dragon): the stars that are between alpharkadin (the polar stars) and the daughters of the bier. Again elsewhere: [II, 681] الصبا ريح مهبها من مطلع الثريا الي بنات نعش [al-ṣabā rīḥ mahabbuhā min maṭlaʿ al-thurayyā ilā banāt naʿsh] Saba, a wind blowing from the rising of the Pleiades to the daughters of the bier, that is, Caecias. Giauhari notes that in the poets one sometimes reads بنى نعش [banī naʿsh] sons of the bier, and of individual stars in the singular ابن نعش [ibn naʿsh] son of the bier ^{(3)}. Hence clear light falls on the passage of Job we are dealing with: Will you lead עיש, the bier, with its sons? ^{(4)} And although the reason for this expression escaped the interpreters, Aben Ezra nevertheless rightly saw that it concerns the sign of seven stars in the north. This sign some call the Bear, others the Wagon, others Helice, others the Septentriones. Nor do I pay heed to the Talmudists, for some of whom עש is זנב טלה, the tail of the Ram; for others רישא דעגלא, the head of the Bull, in the tractate Berachoth fol. 58. b. The Glossator tries to reconcile these opinions, because ראש השור סמוך לזנב טלה שכן הסדר טלה שור תאומים, The head of the Bull is joined to the tail of the Ram, since this is the order of the signs: Ram, Bull, Twins, etc. Nor am I unaware why the Chaldee wanted עיש to be the Pleiades. ערש in Hebrew means to come together and to be gathered, Ioel IV, 11. So it seemed to him that this sign was called עיש as if from coming together. Just as in Greek it is called Πλειὰς [Pleias], ὡς ἐκ πλειόνων ἀςέρων οὖσα [hōs ek pleionōn asterōn ousa]. And in Arabic ثري [thurayy] from the same notion, for ثرا [tharā] means to be multiplied. But why do the Greek translators render Καὶ ἕσπερον ἐπὶ κόμης αὐτοῦ ἄξεις αὐτὸν [Kai hesperon epi komēs autou axeis auton], And the evening star, will you lead him by his hair? For בניה, its sons, they read בנית, hair. And they derived עיש, or עש, from עשי, the word by which the Arabs call evening. In the Vulgate the old editions have And do you make the evening star rise over the ends of the earth? And the new ones over [II, 682] the sons of the earth. But I think both are corrupt. For one should read And do you make the evening star rise over its sons then? That tune [then], though otherwise rare in that version, is nevertheless found at 2 Reg. II, 20. and 3 Reg. XIII, 13. 14. and XVIII, 17. The scribes corrupted the passage because they did not understand what the sons of the evening star were. But the corruption is very ancient, for it had already taken root in the age of Gregory the Great, who evidently read sons of the earth, in book 29 on Job, chapter 17.
